title: Closures
summary: Functions that remember the variables around them.

steps.title: A function remembers where it was born
body: A function can use variables from the scope it was **created** in, even after that scope has finished. That is a **closure**. C# lambdas do the same thing when they capture locals.
let count = 0;                 // private to this call of makeCounter
Nothing outside can touch `count`. Each call to `makeCounter` creates a **new** `count`, so two counters are independent.

steps.explain: `a` and `b` each closed over their own `count`.

steps.title: Closures in loops
body: `let` creates a fresh variable for **each iteration** of a `for` loop, so each closure sees its own value:
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
With the legacy `var` there is only **one** `i` for the whole loop, and every closure sees its final value, `3`. This bug was so common that it is a big reason `let` exists.

code: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) withLet.push(() => i);
for (var j = 0; j < 3; j++) withVar.push(() => j);
steps.explain: `let` gives each iteration its own `i`; `var` shares one `j`, which ends at 3.

steps.prompt: Why is closing over a variable useful for something like a counter or a cache?
options: The state is private: only the returned function can read or change it
It makes the function run faster
It copies the variable so it can never change
It lets other modules modify the variable directly
steps.explain: A closure keeps a live reference to the variable (not a copy), hidden from everyone else. It is how JavaScript did private state before classes had `#private` fields.

steps.title: Bank account
prompt: Write `makeAccount(start: number)` returning an object with three functions that share a private balance:
- `deposit(n)` adds `n` and returns the new balance
- `withdraw(n)` subtracts `n` and returns the new balance, but **throws** an `Error` if `n` is more than the balance
There must be no `balance` property you can change from outside: keep it in a closure.
solution: if (n > balance) throw new Error("Insufficient funds");
template: Dojo.check("balance is a function, not a number", typeof dojoAcc.balance === "function", "balance should be a function");
hints: Each property is an arrow function that reads or changes `balance`.
`throw new Error("Insufficient funds")` before changing anything.
